question:
How should modules be organized so that the software stays easy to maintain, and how can an existing badly structured program be improved without its users noticing any difference?

Answer with a list of guidelines. After each guideline, cite the source it comes from: the path of the SWEBOK file if you have it, otherwise a verbatim quote of at least 8 words from the passage, in the form (source: ...).
answer:
# Summary

Well-structured software organizes modules around single responsibilities, loose coupling, high cohesion, and information hiding. Existing poorly structured programs can be improved through refactoring—reorganizing internals without changing observable behavior—while documentation of design rationale and use of reverse engineering support understanding and safe modification.

# Guidelines

- Apply **information hiding (encapsulation)** so that nonessential implementation details are inaccessible to users of a module, letting them focus on the essential interface elements. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Software Design Principles and Module Organization.md)

- Strive for **loose coupling** between modules: [SWEBOK excerpt 8e09fd042699cb2e6740] to minimize interdependence. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Software Design Principles and Module Organization.md)

- Maximize **cohesion** within each module by organizing its constituents based on their relatedness, so that elements with strong associations are grouped together. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Software Design Principles and Module Organization.md)

- Apply the **single responsibility principle**: [SWEBOK excerpt b39476fe9cb17afc35e8], so each module has one clear purpose. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Component Modularization and Single Responsibility Principle.md)

- Use **separation of concerns** to allow focusing on each concern in isolation, decomposing large software into smaller, independently understandable components. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Separation of Concerns and Modularization in Software Design.md)

- Separate **interface from implementation**: define a component by its public interface so clients can use it without knowing how it is built internally. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Software Design Principles and Module Organization.md)

- Keep modules **small and well-named with well-defined interfaces**: [SWEBOK excerpt 98effe00b8c84e29f8e1]. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Component Modularization and Single Responsibility Principle.md)

- Apply **refactoring** [SWEBOK excerpt 9fbd812fb5aa3b52dd0c], improving internal structure and maintainability while keeping the software's external behavior identical to users. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Maintenance, Evolution, and Quality Assurance/Refactoring and Reverse Engineering in Software Development.md)

- Use **continuous refactoring** to reduce and manage growing complexity over time, especially in iterative/agile development where code quality must be sustained across frequent changes. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Maintenance, Evolution, and Quality Assurance/Refactoring and Reverse Engineering in Software Development.md)

- Use **reverse engineering** to analyze an existing poorly structured program, identify its components and their interrelationships, and create higher-level representations before undertaking restructuring. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Maintenance, Evolution, and Quality Assurance/Refactoring and Reverse Engineering in Software Development.md)

- Use **software visualization tools** (code browsers, quality metrics, technical debt estimation, code smell detection) to explore, analyze, and understand the structure of existing software systems prior to improvement. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Maintenance, Evolution, and Quality Assurance/Software Visualization and Reverse Engineering Tools.md)

- Avoid accumulating **architectural technical debt**: lack of modularity in an initial design adversely affects future development time, maintainability, and requires costly refactoring later. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture_ Foundations, Views, and Patterns/Architectural Design Languages, Decisions, and Technical Debt/Technical Debt and Software Architecture Process.md)

- Apply **uniformity**: produce common solutions to recurring problems across components to maintain consistency throughout the software. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Processes/Modular Design and Core Software Principles/Software Design Principles and Module Organization.md)

- **Record design rationale**, including assumptions, alternatives considered, and trade-offs, because reasons obvious to the current team may be unclear to future maintainers, enhancing long-term maintainability. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Design Concerns, Documentation, and Modeling/Recording Design Rationale for System Maintainability.md)

- Design for **modularity as a measurable maintainability characteristic**: a system composed of independent components minimizes the impact of a change in one component on others. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance Costs, Metrics, and Quality/Software Quality and Maintainability Metrics/Measurable Characteristics of Software Maintainability.md)

- [SWEBOK excerpt 67b13f5c33ecc9e5201b]** to avoid code clones and support future reuse and maintenance. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Construction Techniques and Practices/Software Reuse and Cloud-Based Development/Software Construction for and with Reuse.md)

- Maintain **clear and concise documentation** to aid program comprehension, since [SWEBOK excerpt 1c2a32e2f0e97a5cd93c] before implementing changes. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Maintenance and Configuration Management/Software Maintenance, Evolution, and Quality Assurance/Software Maintenance_ Organization, Configuration, and Quality/Software Maintenance Quality and Program Comprehension Techniques.md)

- Follow **coding and programming standards** consistently across the team; without them, individual styles make integration difficult, systems become defect-prone, and maintenance becomes challenging. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Software Engineering Fundamentals and System Architecture/Operating Systems Fundamentals for Software Engineers/Standards, Guidelines, and Operating Systems Fundamentals.md)

- Apply **abstraction** to focus on information relevant to a particular purpose and identify essential properties, reducing the cognitive burden when understanding or modifying modules. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture Foundations and Design Principles/Software Design Principles and Decision-Making Methods.md)

- Use established **architectural styles and patterns** (e.g., layered, pipes-and-filters, microservices) to structure modules in proven, understandable ways that support maintainability and evolution. (source: /workspace/swebok-v4/root/Foundations of Software Architecture/Software Architecture_ Foundations, Views, and Patterns/Architectural Styles and Design Pattern Catalogs.md)
